stories.headline: Guimarães: Newcastle fans that booed me 'can't delete my history with the club'
stories.summary: Bruno Guimarães has told the Newcastle fans who booed his return to St James Park that they "cannot delete the history I have with the club."
stories.body:
Bruno Guimarães has told the Newcastle fans who booed his return to St James Park that they "cannot delete the history I have with the club."

Guimarães was loudly jeered before, during and after Arsenal's 2-2 draw last Saturday in his first appearance back since a £75 million ($97.7m) summer move to the Gunners.

The 29-year-old spent five seasons on Tyneside and became the first Newcastle captain to lift a trophy in 56 years after beating Liverpool in the 2025 Carabao Cup Final.

Guimarães was a hugely popular figure but the angry reaction from many supporters left the Brazilian in no uncertain terms about where he now stands.

Asked about the contrast between that reaction and the instant backing from Arsenal supporters, Guimarães said on Monday: "The welcome has been amazing, I think they have been so good for me. I want to thank them for their support.

"For the Newcastle fans, I cannot control the fans. They can do whatever they want. The only thing they cannot do is delete the history I have with the club. But I cannot control the fans and that's all."

Guimarães, who has made 15 appearances for the Gunners to date, also hailed the impact Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta is having on his game through a "crazy" attention to detail.

- Arsenal's near-collapse at Newcastle is a wake-up call

- David Raya to be assessed after leaving Arsenal's draw at Newcastle with injury

"Mikel is unbelievable," he added. "As a manager, he is so focused on the small details, the way you control the ball, the way that you cannot be aligned with your opposite side -- some details that I never heard before.

"I just found out listening to him here, very small details, he is so crazy a little bit with these small details and I try to take as much as I can because he is so passionate on the small details.

"He always says to the midfield to not be aligned with the opposition, to give you two or three seconds ahead of them. He showed some clips of me at Newcastle and some clips of me here where he thinks I could do different [things]. I like to keep it a bit more private but he is trying to take me to another level."

stories.headline: Source: Mets agree to 1-year deal with veteran 1B Paul Goldschmidt
stories.summary: The New York Mets continued their spending spree Monday by coming to terms on a one-year deal with first baseman Paul Goldschmidt, a source told ESPN, a day after agreeing to give Tarik Skubal the largest contract ever to a pitcher.
stories.body:
The New York Mets continued their spending spree Monday by coming to terms on a one-year deal with first baseman Paul Goldschmidt, a source told ESPN, a day after agreeing to give Tarik Skubal the largest contract ever to a pitcher.

Goldschmidt checks a box off for the Mets, who sought to add a right-handed-hitting first baseman to platoon with Jared Young this offseason. Goldschmidt, while no longer an MVP-caliber player at 39 years old, continued mashing left-handed pitching in a part-time role with the New York Yankees over the past two years.

In 2025, after signing a one-year deal worth, $12.5 million with the Yankees, Goldschmidt batted .336 with seven home runs and a .981 OPS in 168 plate appearances against lefties. Last season, after signing a one-year, $4 million deal to return to the Bronx in a platoon role, he hit .299 with 11 home runs and a .967 OPS in 183 plate appearances against them.

Goldschmidt, the 2022 NL MVP with the St. Louis Cardinals, is also a universally beloved clubhouse presence lauded for his work ethic and leadership. Ben Rice credited Goldschmidt with helping him transition to first base. Aaron Judge vouched for Goldschmidt to return to the Yankees last year and for his inclusion on Team USA's roster in last year's World Baseball Classic.

He is the latest player to make the jump from the Yankees to the Mets in free agency over the past two years, joining Juan Soto, Clay Holmes, Luke Weaver, and Devin Williams.

Goldschmidt is expected to split time with Young, who had his first extended opportunity in the big leagues at age 30 and capitalized to force himself into the Mets' future. Young, one of the bright spots in a dismal season for the Mets, slashed .275/.339/.454 with nine home runs in 280 plate appearances against right-handers.

Young was given the chance because Jorge Polanco, whom the Mets signed last winter to a two-year, $40 million deal to replace Pete Alonso, was unavailable for most of the season. Achilles, wrist and ankle injuries limited Polanco to 37 games, including just two at first base. He batted .148 with two home runs and a .431 OPS before undergoing season-ending ankle surgery in August.

The Yankees' need for Goldschmidt was not nearly as strong with Giancarlo Stanton set to return to assume most starts at designated hitter if healthy and Rice and Luis Garcia Jr. on the roster to play first base.

On top of landing Goldschmidt and adding Skubal on a nine-year, $450 million deal, the Mets agreed to a three-year, $12 million deal with left-handed reliever Darwinzon Hernández last week and came to terms on an eight-year, $95 million contract extension with a club option for a ninth year with center fielder A.J. Ewing over the weekend.

FanSided first reported the news of Goldschmidt's agreement.

stories.headline: How B.J. Callaghan's long, winding coaching journey led to Nashville success
stories.summary: B.J. Callaghan was a fairly unassuming hire when he took over Nashville. Now he's a Supporters' Shield-winning coach being linked with the USMNT job.
stories.body:
In the spring of 2003, B.J. Callaghan made one of those fateful decisions that can define a life.

He was just months away from finishing his economics degree at Ursinus College, where he had played goalkeeper on the soccer team. It was time to enter the working world.

Or so he thought.

Callaghan went on his first interview and had what amounted to an epiphany. A corporate job wasn't for him. He tested the theory a second time with another job interview. The result was the same. But if he didn't enter the corporate world, what would he do?

"I was taking a minor in coaching while I was in college," Callaghan told ESPN, half joking. "So it was more like there were a lot of signals to me saying, 'You should be a coach.' And I think there was still part of my brain saying, 'Man, I should really be in the business world because that's what you're supposed to do.' And I walked away from those two interviews. I had spoken to my current college coach and told him that, and he kind of laughed and said, 'Yeah, we all kind of know that you should probably be [coaching].'"

Callaghan followed that advice, and over the course of 23 years, hit the motherlode. He worked his way through the youth, college, academy, professional and national team ranks, all the way to his current position as head coach of Nashville SC.

He hasn't been just getting by with NSC, either. One year after leading the Coyotes to the U.S. Open Cup title, their first trophy since the organization joined MLS in 2020, he led Nashville to this year's Supporters' Shield, emblematic of the league's highest points total.

Now he not only has an MLS Cup in his sights, but his name is being bandied about as a possible replacement for Mauricio Pochettino with the U.S. men's national team. Suffice it to say, Callaghan made the right decision.

"You reflect back on the journey and you pick up so many different things, you meet so many different people and so many people along the way invest in you and believe in you and push you and continue to motivate you to keep going," Callaghan said. "I think there is an element of anybody in this profession, you have to have this willingness to maybe take risks a little bit, but at the same time you're doing it because you're betting on yourself and you believe in yourself."

Learning to fly and grind
Part of what gave Callaghan the impetus to be a coach was that it was in the blood to a degree. Callaghan's grandfather, Jack Kraft, was a legendary college basketball coach at Villanova, reaching the NCAA tournament six times and the NIT another five.

That's not to say Callaghan becoming a coach was preordained. It was more a seed that was planted thanks to being part of a sports family. There would be little in the way of pushback from Callaghan's parents about his budding career choice.

"I think you understood that [coaching] was a real thing to have as a profession," Callaghan said about his family. "I think that was much more the confidence to do it and to pursue it and to understand you have to take it really seriously, and you have to work at it and you have to develop it and there's step by step that you have to do."

Callaghan's time at Ursinus proved formative as well. He arrived on campus in August 1999, and as a goalkeeper, made an immediate impression on his teammates. With a height under 6-foot, Callaghan wasn't the most physically imposing goalkeeper, but he compensated in plenty of other ways.

"I guess you would call it fresh energy," said Kevin Poust, 47, a teammate of Callaghan's at Ursinus and now a data analyst. "[Callaghan] was always hyped. He was always positive and very loud. You heard B.J., you knew when he was in the room, that's for sure. And that was every day."

Mike Papenberg, 45, another college teammate of Callaghan's, who is now the athletic director at Palmyra High School in New Jersey, noted that Callaghan's communication was always constructive, and he was more than willing to put his body on the line.

"He was fearless. He's like a pit bull," Papenberg said about Callaghan. "He's not the biggest guy, but he was not afraid of anybody or anything. If he needed to come out and throw a punch to get a ball out off a corner kick or a set piece, he was coming out and throwing that punch."

Callaghan's lack of fear manifested itself in unique ways. Poust recalled how a house they were renting had a flat roof, so Callaghan and his housemates made a big pile of leaves and proceeded to jump off the roof into the pile, taking the old Tom Petty lyric -- "I'm learning to fly, but I ain't got wings" -- a bit too literally.

"We ended up getting in trouble for that," said Poust. "But I remember B.J. flying off and we had to put a mattress [on the pile] because the leaves started to get matted down. He must have bounced like five feet in the air off the mattress because he did a belly flop. No fear right there."

Callaghan's time as a college goalkeeper helped lay the foundation for his coaching mind. He had the best view of the field and was adept at putting his teammates in the positions they needed to be in. He could see things almost before they happened.

"I think the way I looked at the position was trying to understand that it's more about the group in front of you," he said. "There's a little bit of selflessness that comes in because you're counting on 10 other guys to help you before you have to do your job. But at the same time, I think as a coach, there's a massive level of accountability that you have to take. And as a goalkeeper, it's pretty much like, that's the job: accountability."

Armed with that tactical foundation, as well as his lack of fear, Callaghan dove into the coaching ranks. He started at Ursinus before moving to St. Joseph's University as an assistant with the women's program.

He did the same at Villanova before crossing over to the men's program. It helped that he had his wife, Leigh, by his side. Callaghan admits that those early coaching gigs didn't pay well, and Leigh's job in the pharmaceutical industry, not to mention the emotional encouragement she provided, helped him navigate the ups and downs.

"That support, I think, has always been the loving, encouraging, pushing, motivating, whatever you kind of needed at that time," said Callaghan about Leigh. "So there was emotional support. There was obviously family support and glue. And I think there was also, at points in time, it was definitely financial as well. And I think credit to her, she's done that all while being highly successful in her own career."

Hungry, loyal, adaptable
It was at Villanova that Callaghan first crossed paths with current Austin FC manager Jim Curtin. Curtin was a volunteer assistant with the Wildcats, and happened across Callaghan in the "dungeon" of the soccer office.

"He was grinding out film, doing a million different things recruiting-wise and just working his ass off," Curtin said. "Typical B.J."

The two went on to work together again at the Philadelphia Union's academy, and combined to win the 2012 Generation Adidas Cup with the team that had Zack Steffen in goal and Vancouver Whitecaps striker Brian White playing as a right back. For Callaghan, the experience proved to be the perfect incubator for coaches as well as players.

"When you're coaching the academy, one of the good things is you're in an environment where it's OK to make mistakes," Callaghan said. "The players are expected to make mistakes, and guess what, coaches are expected to make mistakes. Your training session isn't going to be perfect every time, but it's OK. It's a place to develop. It's a development environment, and in Philadelphia, it was encouraged. Everybody was there to develop and get better."

When Curtin stepped into the role of manager of the first team in 2014, Callaghan was the first name on his list of possible assistants. The Union have often done things on a budget, so Curtin didn't have a ton of options, but he'd seen enough of Callaghan to know he was precisely what was needed.

"I could have hired a bunch of old buddies that I played with in MLS, but I saw a young guy that was hungry, he was loyal, he was adaptable," Curtin said about Callaghan.

Curtin recalled that Callaghan was versatile, too. He was adept with technology, could break down film, and worked well with players on the field. Curtin rued the fact that Callaghan left the Union for the U.S. men's national team because the Union wouldn't pay him more.

Seizing the opportunity
But Callaghan's strengths proved to be a boon for the USMNT in ways no one could have possibly imagined.

He was part of the staff that took the U.S. to the 2022 World Cup, and he helped Gregg Berhalter cope with the departures of assistants Josh Wolff and Nico Estévez. Callaghan's work ethic was well known by then, but Berhalter began to see growth in his assistant's coaching acumen.

"You see how quickly he takes concepts on, how quickly he can pick up what the opponent is doing," Berhalter said about Callaghan. "There were some real signs that he has a very good tactical mind from that sense. And then the final piece would be how he relates to players. He did a great job as an assistant relating to players and connecting with them."

When Berhalter was out of the U.S. managerial picture for six months in the aftermath of his public feud with the Reyna family, Anthony Hudson initially took over on an interim basis. But then he left to take over Al-Markhiya in the Qatari Stars League.

Callaghan was the next man up, having never been a head coach at the professional level. And he excelled, albeit on an interim basis. At the 2023 Concacaf Nations League, he led the U.S. to the title. His deft personal touch in bringing Gio Reyna back into the national team fold flew under the radar, but it was vital as Reyna recorded two assists in the final, a 2-0 win over Canada.

"I think for me, moving from the club game to the national team really opened my eyes to the robustness and the magnitude and size of what goes on at the national team level," Callaghan said. "And honestly, for the transition from moving to the assistant to the interim, the environment that had been created over the four years that I was there under Gregg, I think was really strong, and the foundation that was built was really good."

Callaghan admitted there was some discomfort in taking on the added demands of a head coach. Media responsibilities were one area he highlighted, although he looked comfortable enough. There was a psychological impact as well.

"It's always like the other half of the day that as assistant coaches, we just stayed continuing to watch video and [studying] the opponent, and the head coach has to go do all of the other parts to that animal," Callaghan said. "I had been exposed to it, but maybe not had the buck stop with me."

The stint got Callaghan noticed, although to hear Nashville GM Mike Jacobs describe it, it wasn't Callaghan's time with the USMNT that made the biggest impression. It was the entire path Callaghan had traveled.

"He worked his way up. He was a grinder," Jacobs said about Callaghan. "To me, he was a risk taker also. Not only in how to play, but in going from Philly to work for the national team. It probably was easier to stay in Philly. So to do that, I think it's a certain type of person who bet on himself. For me, I think knowing all the things about him as a person and then knowing how he wanted to play, we were looking for a game model. It very clearly became just a natural fit for us."

Jacobs' assessment proved accurate. Two trophies in two years, and the possibility of another one under Callaghan, are proof of that. Callaghan has also coached his team to be adaptable. Nashville is adept in possession but can also nail teams on the break.

The Yotes are tough defensively, conceding a league-low 25 goals this season, which was a point of emphasis for Callaghan heading into this campaign.

His flexibility has been tested, too. He noted that opponents have been more conservative defensively than in the past, yet nothing has stopped Nashville, thanks to Callaghan's holistic approach.

"I try to drive this idea that everyone's responsible for everything," Callaghan said. "And I've been out there and I've said everybody attacks and everybody defends. I know it sounds simple, but what it means is we all contribute to everything that happens on the field, and we all have roles and responsibilities for what we want to do. And yeah, we're going to align behind how we all want to do it, but we're all going to be accountable for everything that's on the field together. I think that's how you get them to buy in and how we want to play."

As a result of his success, there's talk that Callaghan is among the candidates for the U.S. managerial opening. Certainly, his time as an interim with the U.S. gives him experience few other candidates have, although one is left to wonder whether the requirements for the job have changed in a way that makes his candidacy less likely. For U.S. Soccer, big foreign names appear to be the federation's focus at the expense of domestic candidates.

Callaghan doesn't sound too perturbed at the hubbub surrounding the position at the moment. He knows where it comes from. He's proud of his path through the U.S. system and the opportunities it has afforded him. He also understands looking too far ahead gets him nowhere. That was driven home in Game 1 of the best-of-three playoff series against FC Cincinnati, in which FCC claimed a 1-0 win on Nashville's turf.

"What's gotten me here is being focused on doing the best job that I can in the opportunities that I've been presented," he said. "I try to push the boundaries of where I'm at in the environment that I'm at, and I spend way more time thinking about the job that I currently have than things that are kind of like ... they're not real. So if it's not real, I'm not going to spend time on that. What's real is my focus here on Nashville."

With the MLS Cup playoffs at hand, for the moment, that's where it will stay.

stories.headline: Real Madrid's Mourinho: Vinícius Jr. 'doesn't have to be MVP' to deliver
stories.summary: Mourinho has backed Vinícius Júnior to "return to his maximum potential" as Real Madrid face PSV Eindhoven in Champions League play.
stories.body:
José Mourinho has backed Vinícius Júnior to "return to his maximum potential" while stressing that the Real Madrid star "doesn't have to be man of the match" to deliver as they face PSV Eindhoven in the Champions League on Tuesday.

Vinícius has served a four-match domestic ban and lost his place to summer signing Yan Diomande in recent weeks, but impressed off the bench in Madrid's 2-1 win over Celta Vigo on Saturday, playing a part in both goals.

Mourinho has confirmed that the Brazil winger will start against PSV as he continues his quest to find his best form, having opted to stay at Madrid and sign a new long-term deal in the summer.

"I think he'll return to his maximum potential," Mourinho said in a news conference on Monday, when asked if Vinícius, 26, can get back to his best. "He's young. Sometimes when players get close to 30, 32 or 33, they aren't able to maintain the ideal physical level.

"There are players who get to that age and they lose their motivation. But Vini is young... He's won everything. He's a very good boy, very empathetic, and that's fundamental. Now he's had a very positive involvement [against Celta]."

Mourinho pointed to the red-card incident against Villarreal on Oct. 10, when Vinicius scored a crucial goal, only to have it disallowed and then be sent off for a hair-pull in the buildup.

"I remember when he changed the game against Villarreal," the coach said. "He scored what would have been a key goal, and then it was ruled out, and he was four games out. Maybe that interrupted his moment of growth, of confidence returning.

"Tomorrow he plays, and we all expect his best version ... But from my side there's no pressure. There's pressure to work hard -- as he's been doing -- and help the team. For me, if he gives everything, he doesn't have to be the man of the match."

Earlier on Monday, Madrid confirmed that forward Endrick had suffered a muscular injury.

The Brazil international, who has been linked with a move in January to secure more game time, played 19 minutes in Madrid's win over Celta.

"Following tests carried out today on our player Endrick by Real Madrid's medical staff, he has been diagnosed with a muscle injury in the adductor of his left leg," the club said in a brief statement. "His recovery will be monitored."

The Great One scored 215 points in 1985-86, 212 in '81-82, 208 in '84-85 and 205 in '83-84. Mario Lemieux came closest to Gretzky, finishing the '88-89 season with 199.

stories.headline: Too-early NBA All-Star picks: The 24 most deserving players right now
stories.summary: So what if the All-Star Game is three months away? We're picking locks and position battles to watch across both conferences.
stories.body:
There's a lot a basketball to be played before the 2027 NBA All-Star Game tips off in Phoenix on Feb. 21, but it's never too early to start surveying the field. With more than a month of regular-season games on the books, here's a rundown of the 12 most deserving candidates from each conference.

These picks were made to reward games played through Sunday and are not intended to be a projection of the rosters, which won't be announced until the new year. Criteria for selection included health, individual production, impact on winning and team success.

Note: Picks conform to the NBA's 2026 mandate of at least eight international players among the 24 selections. The NBA has not yet announced whether last year's "U.S. vs. the World" tournament format will return.

Jump to a conference:

East | West

Eastern Conference All-Stars
Giannis Antetokounmpo, Heat

The "Greek Freak" is back on track in South Beach after a contentious final season with the Milwaukee Bucks. Antetokounmpo, who ranks in the top five leaguewide in scoring and rebounding, is guiding the No. 6 offense that has ironed out some of its wrinkles after a rough opening week.

While there was some cause for concern that a string of lower-body injuries might limit his effectiveness, the 31-year-old forward remains a forces going downhill to the rim. Antetokounmpo is tied for second in dunks and is shooting 72.2% in the basket area. While the two-time MVP has enjoyed perfect availability to start the season, his health deserves continued scrutiny; he has missed or barely played in three of the last four All-Star Games due to injuries.

Cade Cunningham, Pistons

Cunningham has picked up right where he left off during the Pistons' 60-win campaign in 2025-26, with one noticeable improvement. The 25-year-old guard is back as Detroit's offensive playmaker, ranking in the top 10 in scoring and assists. But after struggling with ball-control issues in last year's playoffs, he is averaging a career-low 3.1 turnovers per game. In one of the most impressive individual efforts of the young season, Cunningham posted 52 points, 11 assists and no turnovers in a Nov. 12 double-overtime win over the Washington Wizards.

Thanks to Cunningham's extraordinary offensive impact and an elite team defense, the Pistons have weathered the early-season absence of center Jalen Duren and the offseason departure of Tobias Harris to remain in the East's playoff picture.

Tyrese Maxey, 76ers

The 26-year-old Maxey is the youngest and least accomplished of Philadelphia's four stars, but he would be the first pick if they were all placed into a fantasy draft. The two-time All-Star is the leading scorer and most reliable night-to-night producer for the 76ers, who sit atop the East standings after adding LeBron James and Jaylen Brown during the offseason.

The not-so-secret key to Philadelphia's early success is its 12-0 record in clutch games. Maxey ranks third leaguewide in plus-minus during clutch situations, and his late-game brilliance was pivotal in wins over the Indiana Pacers and the Cleveland Cavaliers.

Jayson Tatum, Celtics

Tatum hasn't quite fully returned to his pre-Achilles tear form, but he's still been awfully good. The six-time All-Star has reestablished himself as the No. 1 option for a potent Boston offense and joins Luka Doncic as the only players averaging at least 26 points, six rebounds and six assists per game.

Tatum's career-high free throw rate is an especially positive indicator for his recovery and a welcome development for the Celtics' outside-in offense, which lost Brown over the summer. After finishing last in free throw attempts in 2025-26, Boston is up to 26th to start this campaign. The Celtics are back in the East's top tier, but there's room to climb higher if Tatum's outside shooting efficiency returns to his career standard.

Karl-Anthony Towns, Knicks

Towns has channeled his disappointment at not receiving a contract extension last offseason into exceptional all-around play. While some of his teammates have battled malaise at the start of what figures to be a grueling title defense, Towns ranks in the top five at his position by player efficiency rating (PER) and win shares.

The 31-year-old center has helped compensate for Mitchell Robinson's offseason departure with a career-high 13.9 rebounds per game, and he leads the NBA with 16 double-doubles. As the Knicks search for more reliable contributions from Josh Hart and Mikal Bridges, Towns has easily boasted the best net rating among New York's starters.

Jalen Brunson, Knicks

The 2026 Finals MVP accepted responsibility for the Knicks' 0-3 start -- "Everything falls on my shoulders," he said -- and he has been instrumental in stabilizing the team in recent weeks. New York's offensive efficiency has fallen well short of the level of its 2025-26 championship campaign, but Brunson has lifted it back into the top 10 over the past 10 games.

Brunson, 30, continues to rank among the league's top 10 scorers and is second in time of possession. So far, he is holding up well despite that high-usage role and his struggling teammates: The three-time All-Star hasn't missed a game and has upped his scoring and 3-point efficiency from last season.

Donovan Mitchell, Cavaliers

The Cavaliers' stars all share blame for the team's thoroughly mediocre start after their conference finals appearance last season. James Harden was playing sluggish and sloppy basketball until he broke out with a 51-point effort against the Pacers on Friday, and Evan Mobley might never escape his cutting "18 and 8" nickname on social media.

Mitchell remains the leading scorer on a top-five Cleveland offense, though his production has slipped slightly as compared with that of last season. While there is a bigger conversation brewing about how Cleveland might pivot if it takes a step back in the playoffs, Mitchell's 24/4/5 averages look good enough to land his eighth straight All-Star selection.

Jaylen Brown, 76ers

When judging Brown's acclimation to Philadelphia after a blockbuster summer trade, one must differentiate between his strange off-court comments and his solid on-court play. Brown's passive-aggressive statements about Tatum blew up in his face when he played poorly in his first head-to-head matchup against his former teammate.

That sequence of events hasn't been representative of Brown's start in Philadelphia. He has slotted in nicely as a sturdy second option for the 76ers, who have kept winning despite poor shooting from Joel Embiid and inconsistent impact from James. Brown occupied a range of offensive roles during his 10 years in Boston, and that flexibility has been an asset since his big move.

Franz Wagner, Magic

The eight names listed above were all no-brainer picks as established All-Stars on winning teams.

Wagner breaks from that pattern as an aspiring first-time selection whose Magic have been digging out of a 2-7 start. The German forward was on track to be an All-Star two years ago before he was sidelined by an oblique injury, and he has been even better this season in Paolo Banchero's absence (ankle).

The 25-year-old Wagner is posting career highs in scoring, rebounds and assists, and he has demonstrated significant growth as a playmaker under new coach Sean Sweeney. After averaging fewer than four assists per game during his first five seasons, Wagner is one of only five players averaging at least eight assists this season.

Filling the final few slots on the East ballot requires some compromises: The top remaining candidates are mostly secondary options on winning teams or leading options on losing teams.

Paul George, Celtics

George has been one of the league's best second options since landing in Boston as part of the return for Brown. The 36-year-old forward has been a natural fit supporting Tatum in the Celtics' 3-point-heavy offense: George is one of only four qualified players shooting better than 40% on at least eight 3-point attempts per game.

While George wasn't a serious All-Star candidate during his two seasons in Philadelphia, he has reentered the conversation thanks to his positive two-way impact. George's plus-16.7 net rating leads Boston's starters and represents one of the best figures among NBA stars. Who saw that coming?

Scottie Barnes is a more imposing player than George and has better individual numbers, but the Toronto Raptors have struggled on both ends in Kawhi Leonard's absence. Barnes' case has also been held back by a groin injury.

Anthony Davis, Wizards

Davis falls neatly into the "leading option on losing team" category because his strong individual play hasn't been enough to propel the new-look Wizards into the East's playoff picture. Still, he joins Antetokounmpo and Victor Wembanyama as the only players averaging at least 25 points and 9 rebounds per game, and Davis has bounced back from an injury-plagued campaign to rank in the top 10 in PER.

Projecting Davis as an All-Star is a conscious decision not to blame him for Trae Young's terrible start in Washington or the Wizards' roster conflicts. Davis has been significantly more productive than Cleveland's Mobley and Miami's Bam Adebayo, who are among the East's other big man candidates. Davis' strong numbers and good health to date beg the question: Will he still be on the Wizards by the time All-Star Weekend rolls around?

Jalen Johnson, Hawks

Philly's James wouldn't qualify for his 23rd consecutive All-Star Game on this ballot. The 41-year-old forward is averaging career lows in points and PER, and he is enduring his worst shooting season since his rookie year. Maxey and Brown are more deserving candidates for the 76ers, who haven't been dominant enough to warrant three selections.

With that said, no one should be surprised if James ultimately lands a spot. The four-time MVP remains one of the league's most popular players, and he was selected as a reserve via the coaches' vote last season despite missing the first 14 games with sciatica.

But the final spot here went to Johnson, who is off to a slower-than-expected start after earning his first All-Star nod last season. The Hawks are a tricky team to reward because they are so deep and balanced: Johnson is their most productive all-around player, guard Nickeil Alexander-Walker is their leading scorer and defensive stopper Dyson Daniels boasts the best net rating in their starting lineup.

Johnson should emerge as Atlanta's most logical representative assuming his poor shooting numbers improve as the season unfolds. If that doesn't happen, Adebayo, Barnes and Miami's Davion Mitchell are the most enticing alternatives.

Western Conference All-Stars
Victor Wembanyama, Spurs

No explanation needed. But let's run through the absurdity of Wembanyama's start anyway.

He is averaging nearly a point per minute, leads the NBA in dunks and is powering a top-five offense. The French center also sits atop the league in blocks for the fourth straight season as the anchor for a top-five defense. With that level of dominance on both ends, it's no surprise that Wembanyama ranks first in PER, win shares, box plus-minus and just about every other advanced metric.

Through his first 17 games, Wembanyama has been a blowout architect with a jaw-dropping plus-28.5 net rating. The only thing preventing him from posting even more ludicrous numbers is San Antonio's cautious decision to limit him to 30.3 minutes per game.

Luka Doncic, Lakers

To this point, Doncic has been the only person preventing Wembanyama from running away with MVP honors. The Slovenian guard's offensive wizardry has the Lakers rivaling the Spurs at the top of the West standings despite losing James and several other veterans over the summer.

The NBA's scoring leader has already torched rival defenses for seven 40-point performances and two 50-pointers, and Doncic's 37.2 points per game average is the highest mark since the 1960s. Doncic, 27, looks fit and motivated after a hamstring injury cut short his 2025-26 campaign, and he has maintained excellent availability while posting one of the highest usage rates in league history.

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Thunder

Gilgeous-Alexander has found this season to be much tougher sledding than his back-to-back MVP campaigns in 2024-25 and 2025-26. After losing three key teammates in offseason trades and three more to major early-season injuries, the ever-steady Canadian guard has done his best to keep Oklahoma City above water as the NBA's second-leading scorer.

What's more, Gilgeous-Alexander is on track to join Wilt Chamberlain and Michael Jordan as the only players to average at least 30 points per game in five straight seasons. But that individual excellence has only translated to an average team offense, and the Thunder will be hard-pressed to make another deep playoff run unless Chet Holmgren (knee) and Cason Wallace (shoulder) are able to recover from their health challenges.

Alperen Sengun, Rockets

Trivia time: Who is the leading scorer for the NBA's most efficient offense?

Somehow, the answer is Sengun, who is posting a career-best 22.1 points per game for a balanced Rockets attack that has all five starters averaging in double digits.

While Fred VanVleet's return from injury has shifted Kevin Durant into a slightly lower-usage role, the 24-year-old Sengun has remained a central part of Houston's offense. The Turkish big man ranks in the top five leaguewide by PER and win shares, and he has dished more assists than any center besides, well ...

Nikola Jokic, Nuggets

Jokic's historic production has shown modest signs of slippage in his age-31 season: He is shooting a career-low 30.2% on 3-pointers, he is scoring less frequently in the basket era, his rebounding rate is down and he has fallen outside the top five in PER and win shares.

While the Serbian center might not finish first or second in MVP voting for the first time since 2019-20, he's still a no-brainer All-Star who squeezes the most possible wins out of an unremarkable supporting cast. Jokic is on pace to lead the league in assists for the second straight season, and Denver's outlook has gradually improved since its lackluster 3-3 start.

Jamal Murray, Nuggets

Like Jokic, Murray has done everything in his power to keep Denver afloat. The Canadian guard has surpassed his longtime teammate to lead the Nuggets in scoring for the first time in his 10-year career, and he is posting career highs in PER and true shooting percentage. Murray's 51/47/88 shooting splits are Stephen Curry-esque.

The sustainability of Denver's approach will draw scrutiny as the season unfolds. Jokic and Murray both rank in the top five leaguewide in minutes per game, and the Nuggets lack credible alternatives to lighten their loads. Even if Denver eventually unravels, there's something gallant about watching Jokic and Murray fight to extend their title-contention window.

Deni Avdija, Trail Blazers

Avdija earned his first All-Star selection last season, but there was reason to be worried that his impact might be blunted by the additions of Damian Lillard and Ja Morant. The Israeli forward has put those concerns to bed with another stellar campaign, striking an excellent partnership with Lillard that has sustained Portland through Morant's early-season hamstring injury.

There's nothing subtle about Avdija's game: He seeks to punish opposing defenses with an onslaught of dribble drives, and he has complemented his typical brass knuckles approach with the best outside shooting season of his career. Other than the Grizzlies, Avdija's Blazers have been the league's biggest overachievers to date.

Ty Jerome, Grizzlies

Barring a rash of injuries, there won't be many spots for first-time selections in the West. Even so, Jerome will be hard to snub if he and Memphis continue this surprising run. The 29-year-old guard hasn't previously been a serious All-Star candidate during a circuitous career that has included multiple stops in the G League, but he has exploded onto the scene as the leading scorer for the NBA's second-ranked offense.

The Grizzlies have emerged as the league's most pleasant surprise thanks to innovative coach Tuomas Iisalo, a strong rookie campaign from Cameron Boozer and vital contributions from the NBA's highest-scoring bench. Jerome stands out within that impressive collective, averaging a career-high 24.8 points per game while ranking in the top 20 leaguewide by PER.

Cooper Flagg, Mavericks

Flagg looks poised to become the fifth No. 1 pick since 2000 to earn All-Star honors in his age-20 season, joining James, Davis, Zion Williamson and Mavericks teammate Kyrie Irving. The Maine native has been on the fast track since high school, and his immediate impact has helped lift the retooling Mavericks into the West's play-in tournament race.

Last season's Rookie of the Year is averaging 24.3 points, 6.3 rebounds and 6.4 assists per game, numbers not posted by such a young player since James and Doncic. Flagg's offensive game is an interesting mix of traditional and modern elements: He is excellent at getting to the free throw line and hitting from the midrange, but his 3-point efficiency and volume at the rim need improvement.

LaMelo Ball, Timberwolves

The Wolves have chugged along as one of the West's best teams even though franchise guard Anthony Edwards played only four games before undergoing knee surgery. Minnesota has two strong candidates to fill Edwards' spot: Ball, a flashy guard who arrived from Charlotte in an offseason trade, and veteran center Rudy Gobert, who has captained the NBA's top-ranked defense.

Both have made indispensable contributions to Minnesota's success. Ball has kept the offense humming and lightened the mood, while Gobert has positioned himself for his 10th All-Defensive selection with steady doses of rim protection and rebounding. Ball, 25, earned the nod here for helping to get the most out of Ayo Dosunmu -- who has stepped into the starting lineup in Edwards' absence -- and forward Jonathan Kuminga, another offseason addition who has exceeded expectations.

Kevin Durant, Rockets

The field for the West's final two All-Star spots has been thinned out by injuries to Edwards, Lakers guard Austin Reaves, Spurs guard Dylan Harper and the Thunder's Jalen Williams and Holmgren. From that group, Reaves is best positioned to make a speedy return and claim a spot.

For now, Durant narrowly edged out Minnesota's Gobert, Portland's Lillard and Phoenix's Devin Booker. The 38-year-old forward has ceded some authority in Houston's offense but has maintained 51/40/88 shooting splits and a healthy plus-8.3 net rating.

The quality of Durant's contributions remains high, even if his 21.0 points per game are the fewest since his rookie campaign. Houston's league-leading offense, which ground down in last year's playoffs, needs Durant's gravity to thrive, and he has led the Rockets in minutes despite being by far the team's oldest player.

Stephen Curry, Warriors

Unlike the other 23 names on this list, Curry is currently sidelined for an extended period due to injury. But the two-time MVP earned a tribute vote on this ballot for his astonishing start to his 18th season.

Before suffering an oblique tear earlier this month, the 38-year-old Curry had turned back the block and was scoring and drilling 3-pointers like he did back in the mid-2010s. What's more, Golden State has been barely functional without its franchise icon: The Warriors are just 4-7 without him, including a 1-4 skid since his injury.

Sadly, Curry's torrid opening month proved too good to be true. If he can't ramp back up to full speed by the time the real All-Star ballots are due, Reaves projects as a worthy replacement. The 28-year-old guard has averaged a career-high 24.7 points per game as Doncic's sidekick in a Lakers offense that has shredded most of its early-season competition.

stories.headline: Qatar Grand Prix 2026: Race start time, how to watch, full schedule, predictions
stories.summary: Formula 1 heads to Qatar for the second leg of its final triple header of the 2026 season.
stories.body:
Formula 1 heads to Qatar for the second leg of its final triple header of the 2026 season.

Max Verstappen fended off his rivals to take a stunning victory under the lights at the Las Vegas Grand Prix last time out.

McLaren's Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri took the final spots on the podium.

So you don't miss a thing, here's everything you need to know for the 22nd round.

- Max Verstappen mocks George Russell in brutal outburst: 'So far below my level'

- Lewis Hamilton, Charles Leclerc 'unmanageable' - Ferrari boss

- Max Verstappen, George Russell's latest war of words unlikely to stay in Vegas

Qatar Grand Prix schedule
All times in GMT

Friday, November 27

Practice One: 1.30 p.m. - 2.30 p.m.

Practice Two: 5 p.m. - 6 p.m.

Saturday, November 28

Final Practice: 2.30 p.m. - 3.30 p.m.

Qualifying: 6 p.m. - 7 p.m.

Sunday, November 29

Qatar Grand Prix: 4 p.m.

How to watch

Every practice and qualifying session as well as the race itself will be available to watch on Sky Sports F1. The sessions are also on Sky Sports Main Event.

For non-subscribers, highlights of the Qatar Grand Prix will be on free-to-air television on Channel 4.

In the U.S., subscribers can watch every session on Apple TV, via a new F1 channel on the platform.

Lusail Circuit

The Qatar Grand Prix takes place under the floodlights at the Lusail Circuit. It is one of the most demanding on the calendar with long straights and sweeping high-speed corners coupled with intense heat and humidity, making conditions for the cars and drivers difficult.

It was originally built as a motorbike circuit before it joined the F1 calendar in 2021 on a 10-year contract. Qatar did not host a race in 2022 as they focused on the FIFA World Cup.

Qatar Grand Prix

Circuit: Lusail International Circuit; Lusail, Qatar

Previous winners in Qatar

2021: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2023: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2024: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2025: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Other key stats

First F1 race: 2021

Laps: 57 laps of 5.4km

Lap record: 1:22.384, Lando Norris (2024)

Most wins: Verstappen (2023, 2024 and 2025). Lewis Hamilton (2021) is the only other winner.

Most poles: Hamilton (2021), Verstappen (2023), George Russell (2024) and Piastri (2025) have each taken pole.

Weather forecast

The weather for the Qatar Grand Prix is forecast to be sunny with a gentle breeze across the weekend. It's a night race so conditions are dry with highs of 24°C on Sunday.

What happened last time out?

McLaren's Piastri pipped teammate Norris to pole position as the battle for the world title continued with two races remaining.

During the race, Red Bull's Verstappen benefited from a McLaren strategy error to win his seventh race of the season, taking the three-way title race to the season finale in Abu Dhabi.

Piastri was leading the race and Norris was running in third, but the Papaya team decided against pitting under the Safety Car. Piastri ended the race in second, with Norris in fourth.

Who will win this year?

Verstappen looked unstoppable in Las Vegas and will be targeting his fifth win of the season in Qatar.

Mercedes' Russell was well in the mix last time out but will be looking to respond after Verstappen said the Englishman was "so far below his level" as their feud intensified.

Both teams look strong, so the rivalry could well continue in Qatar. Drivers up and down the grid will also be limited to 27 laps on each set of tyres, which will play massively into teams' strategies.

Tensions between Ferrari teammates Hamilton and Charles Leclerc continue to heat up after boss Fred Vasseur labelled them "unmanageable."

Don't count out new world champion Kimi Antonelli who is always one to watch after an impressive season.

stories.headline: Heeney headlines returning Swans at pre-season training
stories.summary: After months of off-field turmoil in the fallout from the Pullman Hotel scandal, the Sydney Swans have welcomed back four AFL players for pre-season training.
stories.body:
The Sydney Swans have welcomed back their embattled AFL quartet to training after months of off-field turmoil following the Pullman Hotel scandal.

Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice signalled their intent to resurrect their playing careers by taking part in the club's first-to-fourth-year pre-season training on Monday.

High-profile forward Tom Papley was also in attendance at Sydney's Bat and Ball Oval after being slapped with a three-game ban by the AFL for a positive roadside drug test.

Monday's session marked the first time Heeney, Warner, Bice and Jordon have officially trained with the Swans since serving a season-ending suspension for what the club termed a "serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards".

That AFL-endorsed suspension was also served by now-North Melbourne player Nick Blakey.

Separate from the bans, Heeney, Warner, Jordon and Blakey were under investigation after three women made reports of sexual assault to Victoria Police.

Police have since confirmed the players would not be charged due to insufficient evidence.

Civil claims are still being prepared against relevant parties.

Monday's session was a relaxed affair, with the club also welcoming draftees Caylen Murray, Mason McGroder, Mitchell Knevitt and Brady Wright.

Players undertook the usual pre-season conditioning programs, doing running drills before moving on to contest work and a short match simulation.

It wasn't the first time Heeney, Warner, Jordon and Rice had trained with teammates, having done informal sessions at Centennial Park.

Papley, one of the team's most experienced players, returned to training as he prepares to face Waverley Local Court for driving with a suspended licence on November 26.

The 30-year-old was pulled over by NSW Police for a random roadside drug test on November 2, with checks revealing his licence was suspended due to non-payment of a parking fine.

The initial roadside test returned a positive reading, and a secondary sample of oral fluid was taken.

That secondary sample returned a positive roadside test for the presence of cocaine and MDMA.

On top of his AFL ban for conduct unbecoming, Papley was fined $722 by police and his licence will be suspended for three months.

Papley spent most of Monday's training session with the rehabilitation group alongside fellow forwards Logan McDonald and Hayden McLean after undergoing surgery on both knees.

He suffered a grade-two medial collateral ligament strain in his right knee in the club's preliminary final loss to Fremantle, before undergoing an arthroscopy on his left knee to address a historic issue.

Papley will miss all pre-season matches and the club's opening rounds against Geelong, Essendon and GWS.
